source_read: PMC full text PMC6006320 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6006320/), read in the app's browser in a tab of my own: abstract, every section, Table 1 with its notes (rendered as text), the Figure 1-3 legends, the author affiliations, funding and competing-interest statements. The heading hierarchy and paragraph counts were checked in the page structure. Figures 1-3 are images (values not extracted beyond the text and legends); Supplementary Table 1 not read.

key_findings.note: Methods and materials > Participants 1st paragraph (41 and 37, not seeking treatment, advertisements, payment, 22 on the GCRC research ward, 6.9 days, SD 2.7, range 3-30, urine tests at entry and on testing days).

Table 1 (employed yes/no 24/17 and 10/27; smokers 14/27 and 34/3) and Results > Group comparisons 1st paragraph. The gender split (21/20 vs 25/12) gives chi-square p = 0.14 (recomputed), consistent with the text's 'did not significantly differ'.
Table 1; Participants 2nd paragraph; Group comparisons 1st paragraph (ps > 0.35).

Table 1; Group comparisons 2nd paragraph; Academic records. Recomputed: standardized difference in grades 0.62. The standardized-test comparison reproduces exactly from the printed means and SDs (t = 1.37, p = 0.178).

Predictive modeling 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend. Recomputed: 3.732/sqrt(37) = 0.614. Decomposition reproduced with smoking coded 1 for smokers: predicted control mean 0.001, predicted methamphetamine mean -0.301 (grades -0.162, smoking -0.115, parental income -0.022, age -0.002); actual -0.639 from the two subgroup means; the model accounts for 47% of the raw gap.
Predictive modeling 4th paragraph (ps > 0.10 for attention and memory).
Predictive modeling 5th paragraph. Recomputed: both r and p pairs fit n = 26 best (p 0.0446 and 0.0103 at n = 26; 0.015 and 0.002 at n = 37); withdrawal fits n = 37 (p 0.0286).

Predictive modeling 6th and 7th paragraphs. 6.888/sqrt(24) = 1.406 and 3.776/sqrt(28) = 0.714 recomputed. Worth adding: the standardized-test model was fitted in only 19 controls (R2 0.46, p = 0.017), so d 1.41 rests on a smaller model base than the main analysis; the GPA-matched groups differed by p = 0.58 on GPA.
Cortical thickness 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 3 legend (N = 31). Correlation p values reproduce for n = 31 (0.061 and 0.026).
Methods and materials > Measures/procedures > Cognitive battery (the authors also say standardizing to controls is a scale change that does not influence the predictive modeling).

key_findings.correction: Replace 'effects of methamphetamine cannot be disentangled from other drug use' with 'it is difficult to disentangle effects of methamphetamine from other substance use, and the data lack the detail to tell whether this leads to under- or overestimation'. The authors' word is 'difficult'; 'not possible' applies only to deciding between the two directions with these data (Discussion 4th paragraph). The 7th-paragraph limitations are confirmed as listed.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E fits a cross-sectional exposure comparison. I agree with every domain and with overall high. Confounding high rather than very high: the design does address premorbid differences through pre-use grades, but other substance use disorders (alcohol 26 vs 9, cocaine 12 vs 0, marijuana 21 vs 9, other 9 vs 0) are not modelled, and the within-group test that past diagnoses were unrelated to scores (ps > 0.35) has little power (6 without any past diagnosis).

risk_of_bias_domains.note: Blinding of testers is not reported (Cognitive battery paragraph).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The quotation is verbatim from the abstract, and the abstract hedges it in the same sentence ('and/or a failure to develop normative cognitive abilities'; other drug use and unidentified factors 'likely contribute'). The limitations deny a causal demonstration (Discussion 7th paragraph). A case for 'substantial' exists because of the two overreaches listed under missed; I would still rate minor, because the paper states its own limits plainly.

missed: Effect-size metric (Discussion 3rd and 6th paragraphs). The authors call the paired d values 'medium' (0.69, 0.46) and 'moderate' (0.54) and 'consistent with meta-analytic data'. These are paired standardized differences: the mean shortfall divided by the SD of individual shortfalls, about 0.55 composite units here by editors' calculation (0.338/0.61). Meta-analytic d values are between-group differences in pooled-SD units, so the comparison is not like-for-like. In the composite's own units the mean shortfall is about 0.34 (predicted -0.30, actual -0.64; editors' calculation).

Discussion 2nd paragraph says confidence in the causal reading 'is strengthened' because the groups were well matched on demographics. Demographic matching does not touch what the model leaves out (other substance use disorders, unmodelled premorbid differences). This could join the card's list of gaps.

Sample overlap (Participants 1st paragraph): the cognitive data had not been published before, so this is the same laboratory as Simon et al. (2010) but not the same participants for cognition. About 70% of the sample overlaps with Okita et al. (2017) for cortical thickness. This matters for replication counting: same team, new sample.
Locator detail: in the HTML, 'Structural MRI' is a subsection of Methods and materials, not of Measures/procedures (the card's attrition field writes 'Measures/procedures > Structural MRI').
